title: The Agent Native Company — Rick Blalock, Agentuity

primary.label: AI Product, UX & Human Factors
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 76%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk focuses on how humans collaborate with, supervise, and orchestrate AI agents in a company, covering hiring, onboarding, org structure, and the human-as-conductor paradigm.

summary:
Rick Blalock from Agentuity presents on agent-native (AI-native) companies, defining them as organizations built from the ground up with AI agents at the core of product, operations, and culture—not as bolt-on features but as the engine driving everything forward. He opens with a vision of the future workday: arriving at your desk, checking what your AI agent coworkers accomplished overnight, reviewing their pull requests, and kicking off new tasks. He shares Agentuity's own experience where agents named Devon handle coding tasks and bugs from Linear, a content marketing agent optimizes copy and schedules social posts, and another agent writes changelogs and documentation from GitHub activity. The routine becomes: mornings reviewing agent output and kicking off tasks, lunchtime reviewing accumulated PRs, collateral, and emails.

He draws a clear distinction between AI-enhanced and AI-native companies. AI-enhanced businesses use AI sporadically for efficiency gains but would still function if AI were removed—likened to a car with driver assist. AI-native companies are on autopilot directed by humans; removing agents would cause productivity collapse, rising costs, and products that feel outdated. This model is a fundamental redefinition of team-building, workflow design, and hiring, comparable to the Industrial Revolution or the advent of the automobile.

Core attributes include: AI everywhere across departments with agent interfaces and inter-departmental handoffs; humans shifting from cogs to conductors orchestrating intelligent systems; flatter org charts trending toward human-AI networks with shrinking middle management; experimentation culture realized through AI handling routine work; and self-learning agents that compound value over time. He cites Cognition's tool documenting their codebase over months as a superpower. Titles will combine domain expertise with AI know-how—AI engineer, AI customer lead—across every department.

Hiring must shift toward AI fluency, curiosity, and adaptability. Blalock compares AI fluency to keyboard skills: once debatable, now universally expected. In interviews, unfamiliarity with AI raises immediate warning flags. VP hiring, traditionally driven by professional networks, now spotlights whether candidates can guide agents and bring in AI-fluent people. Onboarding changes too—new hires may spend their first weeks setting up their agent stacks, with engineers attached to teams to ensure agents are operational.

He closes urging founders and tech leaders to embrace this paradigm shift, check outdated experience at the door, and reimagine org charts, roles, and culture from first principles. The shift creates friction but can become an unfair advantage.

sections.title: Introduction and Vision of the Agentic Workday
sections.summary: Rick introduces agent-native companies and envisions arriving at work to check agent co-workers' overnight progress rather than email. Shares Agentuity examples: delegating to Devon for pull requests during standups, pinging content marketing agent for channel adjustments, and a startup posting an Agent Manager job on X.

sections.title: AI Enhanced vs AI Native
sections.summary: Contrasts AI-enhanced (car with driver assist, still functions without AI) vs AI-native (autopilot directed by humans, breaks without agents). Defines agent-native as built from ground up with AI at core of product, operations, and culture. Removing agents causes sadness, slower movement, higher costs, and outdated products.

sections.title: What Makes a Company Agent Native
sections.summary: Core attributes: AI everywhere across departments with agent interfaces and handoffs; humans as conductors not cogs; flatter org charts trending to human-AI networks with shrinking middle management; experimentation culture realized through AI handling routine work; self-learning agent evolution. Cites Cognition's tool as a compounding superpower that documented their codebase over months.

sections.title: The Typical Agentic Workday and Content Marketing Swarms
sections.summary: Describes the daily routine: mornings reviewing agent output and kicking off tasks, lunchtime reviewing PRs, collateral, and emails from agents. Devon handles bugs and doc issues from Linear automatically with PRs ready. Content marketing swarms orchestrate multiple agents for copy optimization, social posting timing, and auto-scheduling via Typefully. Every employee becomes a lead manager of their AI agent counterparts. Titles will combine domain expertise with AI know-how across all departments.

sections.title: Rethinking Hiring, Onboarding, and Closing
sections.summary: Hiring must prioritize AI fluency, curiosity, and adaptability—compared to keyboard skills once debatable but now expected. Interview skepticism arises when candidates lack AI familiarity. VP hiring shifts from network value to AI fluency. Onboarding changes: new hires may spend initial weeks setting up agent stacks with engineers attached to teams. Blalock closes comparing this shift to the automobile's economic impact, cites a PWC report warning that small efficiency gains mean falling behind, urges founders to check outdated experience at the door and reimagine from first principles, and asks: is your company using AI or ready to be built around AI?
